lede: A body that is not accelerating has forces that cancel exactly. That single idea turns a picture of four forces into two ordinary equations, and those equations are where most of the marks in a Unit 2 forces question live.
can: Recognise when a body is in equilibrium and say what that means for its forces
Write two component equations, with every force in each of them
Find an unknown force or angle on the flat, on a slope and at a point

md: Stand still and two forces act on you: the Earth pulls you down, the floor pushes you up, and they match. Nothing is left over.

alt: A particle at O held still by three forces: 24 N horizontally to the right, 7 N vertically downwards, and 25 N up and to the left at 16.26 degrees to the horizontal.

caption: Three forces that add to nothing: 25 N up and to the left at 16.26° to the horizontal.

md: A particle is in equilibrium when the resultant of the forces on it is zero. Not small: zero. So it stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line: nothing is left over to change its motion.

**Shown, for the picture:** the 25 N force splits into $25\cos 16.26° = 24$ N left and $25\sin 16.26° = 7$ N up.
**Across:** $24 - 24 = 0$. **Up and down:** $7 - 7 = 0$.

prompt: A particle is in equilibrium under three forces. What is the resultant of those forces?
options: zero
the largest of the three
the sum of the three sizes
explain: Equilibrium means the forces cancel in every direction, as the three in the picture did across and up: nothing is left over, so the resultant is zero. If anything were left over the particle would accelerate.

md: A zero resultant means zero in every direction, so choose two perpendicular ones and write an equation for each: horizontal and vertical on the flat, along and across a slope. Two equations find two unknowns.

title: Why two directions are enough
md: Any force can be rebuilt from its parts along two perpendicular directions, so if both totals are zero nothing is left in any direction. A third equation would only repeat the first two.
**Shown:** for a rope pulling with 45 N at 35°, $45\sin 35° = 25.81$ N is one component: the start of the method. The marks follow the equation that puts every vertical force in, $R + 25.81 = 120$.

prompt: A candidate resolves one force on a body in equilibrium and writes down its vertical component, then stops. What is missing?
options: an equation setting the total of every vertical force to zero
the horizontal component of that same force
the mass of the body
answer: an equation setting the total of every vertical force to zero
explain: A single component is where the method starts, as the line above showed; the marks that follow are for the equation with every vertical force in it, set equal to zero.

text: 3. Where the two equations come from

md: Add up the horizontal parts of all the forces to get $X$, and the vertical parts to get $Y$. The resultant is the diagonal of the rectangle they make, so by Pythagoras its size is $\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$. That is zero only when $X = 0$ and $Y = 0$ together: which is exactly the pair of equations.
**Shown:** totals of $X = 6$ N and $Y = 8$ N give a resultant of $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$ N, so the body is not in equilibrium. Only $X = 0$ and $Y = 0$ give $0$.

prompt: The horizontal parts of the forces on a particle add to 0 N and the vertical parts add to 12 N upwards. What is the size of the resultant, in newtons?
explain: The resultant has size $\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, as in the line above. Here $X = 0$ and $Y = 12$, so it is $\sqrt{0 + 144} = 12$ N: one equation holding is not enough, both must.

caption: A 45 N pull at 35° on a 12 kg block that does not move.

md: The commonest way marks go is an equation with too few terms. A rope at an angle has a part that lifts, so the vertical equation holds three forces: the reaction, the rope's lift and the weight.

**Resolving vertically:** $R + 45\sin 35° = 120$, so $R = 94.19$ N.
**Resolving horizontally:** $F = 45\cos 35° = 36.86$ N.
Writing $R = 120$ ignores the rope's lift; writing $R = 45\sin 35°$ ignores the weight.

title: What the reports keep saying
md: Equations with only two terms are described as very common, and a large number of candidates never set up the vertical equation at all. Both lose the marks that the equation itself carries.

prompt: A block of weight 60 N rests on a table and a rope pulls it with a vertical component of 24 N upwards. What is the normal reaction, in newtons?
explain: Three forces have vertical parts, as for the block above: the reaction and the rope's 24 N together hold up the 60 N weight. Resolving vertically, $R + 24 = 60$, so $R = 36$ N.

text: 5. Smooth slope: a rope holds it

alt: A box of mass 18 kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at 24 degrees by a rope along the slope: T up the slope, R at right angles to it, and 180 N straight down.

caption: A 18 kg box held still on a smooth 24° slope by a rope.

md: On a slope the useful pair of directions is along the surface and at right angles to it, because two of the three forces already lie along them. Only the weight has to be resolved.

**Along the slope:** $T = 180\sin 24° = 73.21$ N.
**At right angles:** $R = 180\cos 24° = 164.44$ N, less than the weight, since $\cos 24°$ is less than 1.

prompt: A box is held at rest on a smooth slope by a rope parallel to the slope. How does the normal reaction on it compare with its weight?
options: it is smaller than the weight
it is equal to the weight
it is larger than the weight
answer: it is smaller than the weight
explain: Only the part of the weight pressing into the slope has to be balanced, $mg\cos\alpha$, as with the 18 kg box above; $\cos\alpha$ is less than one for any real slope, so the reaction is smaller than the weight.

text: 6. On a rough slope: friction holds it

alt: A crate of mass 7 kg at rest on a rough slope inclined at 18 degrees with nothing attached: friction F up the slope, R at right angles to it, and 70 N straight down.

caption: No rope: friction up the slope is what holds it.

md: Take the rope away and a box on a rough slope can still sit there. Friction has taken the rope's place, so it acts up the slope and matches the part of the weight pulling the box down it.

**Along the slope:** $F = 70\sin 18° = 21.63$ N, up the slope.
**At right angles:** $R = 70\cos 18° = 66.57$ N.

prompt: A crate rests on a rough slope with nothing attached to it. Which force balances the component of the weight acting down the slope?
options: the force due to friction, acting up the slope
the normal reaction
the whole weight
answer: the force due to friction, acting up the slope
explain: The reaction is at right angles to the slope, so it can do nothing along it; friction is the only force left that lies along the surface, and it acts up the slope, as in the picture.

text: 7. At a point: two equations, two unknowns

alt: A particle at O held in equilibrium by 21 N horizontally to the right, 20 N vertically downwards, and a force P up and to the left at an angle theta to the horizontal.

caption: The third force's size and angle are both unknown.

md: When an unknown force P acts at an unknown angle θ, write its two parts as $P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ and let the two equations find them. The papers set this shape at a point with three or four forces.

**Horizontally:** $P\cos\theta = 21$.
**Vertically:** $P\sin\theta = 20$.

prompt: A particle is held in equilibrium by 9 N to the right, 12 N downwards and a force P at an angle θ above the horizontal, to the left. Which pair of equations is right?
options: P cos θ = 9 and P sin θ = 12
P sin θ = 9 and P cos θ = 12
answer: P cos θ = 9 and P sin θ = 12
explain: The angle is measured from the horizontal, so the horizontal part of P takes the cosine and balances the 9 N, and the vertical part takes the sine and balances the 12 N, as in the two lines above.

text: 8. See it done: P and θ

md:
**Pythagoras:** $P^2 = 21^2 + 20^2 = 841$, so $P = 29$ N.
**Divide:** $\tan\theta = \dfrac{20}{21}$, so $\theta = 43.6°$.
$P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose longest side is $P$.

title: FM Mechanics resolving around a point
why: Taught straight against this specification. Watch the two directions being named in writing before either equation is formed.

prompt: A particle is held in equilibrium by 9 N to the right, 12 N downwards and a third force. What is the magnitude of the third force, in newtons?
explain: The third force's parts balance the other two, so they are 9 N and 12 N: the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle, as in the Pythagoras line above. $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ N.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Lami's theorem, the triangle of forces and friction as $F = \mu R$ are A-level methods. CCEA's equilibrium questions are solved with two component equations, and friction is given or found from the balance.

md: Equilibrium does not mean stationary. A body moving at constant velocity is not accelerating, so $F = ma$ gives a resultant of zero and the forces balance exactly as they do at rest. *At rest*, *held still* and *moving with constant velocity* are one instruction.

**Along the ground:** $F = 44\cos 20° = 41.35$ N.
**Vertically:** $R = 50 - 44\sin 20° = 34.95$ N.

prompt: A crate is being dragged across a floor at a constant velocity of 2 m/s. What is true of the forces on it?
options: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
they do not balance, because it is moving
the driving force must be the largest
answer: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
explain: Constant velocity means the speed is not changing, so $a = 0$ and $F = ma$ makes the resultant zero, as for the sledge above, where the friction matched the pull's part along the ground exactly.

md: **An angle to the vertical** (2024, 2026). A force is given at an angle to the vertical, not the horizontal. First line: its vertical part now takes the cosine and its horizontal part the sine.
**Shown:** 40 N at 20° to the vertical has a vertical part $40\cos 20° = 37.59$ N and a horizontal part $40\sin 20° = 13.68$ N.

prompt: A force of 30 N acts at 50° to the vertical. Which expression gives its horizontal part?
explain: Measured from the vertical, the side next to the angle is the vertical part, so the vertical part takes the cosine and the horizontal part the sine, as the 40 N force above showed: $30\sin 50°$.

md: **Mark the forces** (2019). A part asks you to mark the forces on the diagram before any equation. First line: each force with an arrow and a label, the weight included.

**One way still, the other moving** (2019, 2023). A block pulled at an angle is in equilibrium vertically, which gives the reaction, while along the floor $F = ma$. **Shown:** 10 kg on a smooth floor, 40 N at 30°: $R = 100 - 40\sin 30° = 80$ N, and $40\cos 30° = 10a$, $a = 3.46$ m/s².

prompt: A block is pulled along a smooth floor by a rope at an angle. Part (i) asks for the normal reaction and part (ii) for the acceleration. Which part uses equilibrium?
options: Part (i): vertically nothing accelerates
Part (ii): the block moves along the floor
Neither part
explain: The block does not rise or sink, so vertically the forces balance and give the reaction, as in the line above; along the floor it speeds up, so part (ii) uses $F = ma$.

md: **A steady speed** (2023). Moving at constant velocity is equilibrium too, so the forces along the floor balance and friction is the pull's part along it.

caption: Two unknowns, one along each direction, and angles to both lines.

md: The hardest shape so far (2024, 2026) puts four forces at a point: one unknown horizontal, one unknown vertical, and two known forces at angles, one to the vertical and one to the horizontal.

**Vertically:** $W = 30\cos 35° - 16\sin 25° = 17.81$ N.
**Horizontally:** $P = 30\sin 35° + 16\cos 25° = 31.71$ N.

prompt: Four forces hold a point still: an unknown P horizontal, an unknown W vertical and two known forces at angles. Why can each unknown be found from one equation?
options: Each unknown lies along one of the two directions, so it appears in one equation only
The two known forces cancel each other
W is always the largest force
answer: Each unknown lies along one of the two directions, so it appears in one equation only
explain: P is horizontal, so it has no vertical part, and W is vertical, so it has no horizontal part; each equation above holds just one unknown, as the two lines showed.

md:
Say what equilibrium means, and read at rest, held still and constant velocity as one instruction.
Write a complete equation in each of two perpendicular directions, every force included.
Resolve along and across a slope, with friction holding a body still on a rough one.
Find an unknown force and angle at a point, with angles to either line.
Spot the twists: the diagram, still one way and moving the other, a steady speed.

An equilibrium part is worth 2 or 3 marks and is worded 'Calculate the value of' or 'Calculate the normal reaction'. The first mark is for naming the direction you are resolving in and writing a complete equation; the last is for the value to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Write 'resolving vertically' on its own line, then list every force that has a vertical part.
